correctness.rationale: For each nonzero real scalar \(f\), the factor energy equals \(-|f|^2\), violating every positive lower frame bound. In the tensor product, \((-I)\otimes(-I)=I\) and the single tensor block gives \(|f\otimes g|^2\), hence tensor Parseval bounds \(A=B=1\); in one dimension all tensor vectors are simple. The primary article distinguishes \(GB(H)\) from \(GB^+(H)\) and prints \(T,U\in GB(H)\) in its definition and Theorem 4. For the repaired positive branch, a tensor lower bound \(A\|f\|^2\|g\|^2>0\) and factorization force strictly positive energies on nonzero vectors; fixing \(g_0\ne0\) yields factor bounds after division by \(q_K(g_0)>0\), and symmetrically for the other factor. Nonnegative real factor energies are sufficient, not a claimed necessary characterization for complex controls.

value.rationale: This is a decisive correction to the claimed tensor-product characterization, not an arbitrary negative example: the smallest admissible tensor frame refutes the exact reverse implication and exhibits the missing sign logic; the positive-branch repair gives a useful criterion for safely applying the theorem.

final_claim: The reverse implication of Theorem 4 in Ghosh--Samanta (2021), under its printed arbitrary-invertible-control definition, is false: taking \(H=K=\mathbb R\), one identity analysis block in each factor and controls \(T=T_1=I\), \(U=U_1=-I\) makes both factor controlled energies negative but the tensor controlled frame Parseval. If both factor quadratic energies are real and nonnegative, the reverse implication is valid by fixing one nonzero vector and dividing by a strictly positive factor energy.
limitations: Real one-dimensional counterexample suffices to refute the general theorem; a full complex phase-sign classification is not asserted.
The sufficient positivity repair is not a characterization of all possible controls or spectra.
